metadata.title: Taylor series expansions for the entropy rate of Hidden Markov Processes

extraction_notes.note: Thm. 1.1 of Han & Marcus is only applied inside the proof of Theorem 2 (not stated), and the conjecture of ZKD1 that Theorem 1 proves is only mentioned, so neither is a node.
assumption or definition: one sentence both assumes $M>0$ and introduces $\pi$; kept as assumption, with term edges from it to the nodes that use $\pi$.

two_thms_sec.section: From Finite system entropy to entropy rate

nodes.name: Finite-state stationary Markov process
nodes.statement: Let $\{X_N\}$ be a finite state stationary markov process over the alphabet $\Sigma = \{1,\ldots,s\}$.

nodes.name: Noisy observation process
nodes.statement: Let $\{Y_N\}$ be its noisy observation (on the same alphabet).

nodes.name: Markov transition matrix and emission matrix
nodes.statement: Let $M = M_{s \times s} = \{m_{ij}\}$ be the Markov transition matrix and $R = R_{s \times s}$ be the emission matrix, i.e. $P(X_{N+1} = j | X_N = i) = m_{ij}$ and $P(Y_N = j | X_N = i) = r_{ij}$.
nodes.statement_short: $M=\{m_{ij}\}$ is the transition matrix of $X$ and $R=\{r_{ij}\}$ the emission matrix from $X_N$ to $Y_N$.

nodes.name: Strictly positive Markov matrix
nodes.statement: We assume that the Markov matrix $M$ is strictly positive ($m_{ij} > 0$), and denote its stationary distribution by the (column) vector $\pi$ ,satisfying $\pi^t M = \pi^t$.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is strictly positive; $\pi$ denotes its stationary distribution, $\pi^t M=\pi^t$.

nodes.name: Hidden Markov Process (HMP)
nodes.statement: The process $Y$ can be viewed as a noisy observation of $X$, through a noisy channel. It is known as a {\it Hidden Markov Process (HMP)}, and is determined by the parameters $M$ and $R$.
nodes.genus: noisy observation of $X$, through a noisy channel

nodes.name: Block notation $[X]_i^j$
nodes.statement: More formally, for $i \leq j$, let $[X]_i^j$ denote the vector $(X_i,\ldots,X_j)$.

nodes.name: Entropy rate
nodes.statement: Then the entropy rate $\bar{H}(Y)$ is defined as : \begin{equation} \bar{H}(Y) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{H([Y]_1^N)}{N} \end{equation} \noindent Where $H(X) = -\sum_X P(X) \log P(X)$; Here and throughout the paper we use natural logarithms, so the entropy is measured in {\it NATS}, and also adopt the convention $0 \log 0 \equiv 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Entropy rate $\bar{H}(Y)=\lim_N H([Y]_1^N)/N$ with Shannon entropy $H(X)=-\sum P\log P$ in nats.

nodes.name: Entropy rate as limit of conditional entropies
nodes.statement: The entropy rate can also be computed via the conditional entropy as: $\bar{H}(Y) = \lim_{N \to \infty} H(Y_N | [Y]_1^{N-1})$, since for a stationary process the two limits exist and coincide (\cite{Cover}).
conclusions: the two limits exist and coincide

nodes.name: Conditional entropy
nodes.statement: The conditional entropy $H(Y|X)$ (where $X,Y$ are sets of r.v.s.) represents the average uncertainty of $Y$, assuming that we know $X$, that is $H(Y|X) = \sum_{x} P(X = x) H(Y | X=x) $.

nodes.name: Chain rule for entropy
nodes.statement: By the chain rule for entropy, it can also be viewed as a difference of entropies, $H(Y|X) = H(X,Y) - H(X)$, which will be used later.

nodes.name: Symmetric binary HMP
nodes.statement: The expansion coefficients were given in \cite{ZKD1}, for the symmetric binary case. In this case, the matrices $M$ and $R$ are given by : $$ M = \begin{pmatrix} 1-p & p \\ p & 1-p \end{pmatrix} \: \:, \: \: R = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\epsilon & \epsilon \\ \epsilon & 1-\epsilon \end{pmatrix} $$ \noindent and the process is characterized by the two parameters $p,\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric binary HMP: $M$ flips with probability $p$, $R$ flips with probability $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: High-SNR regime
nodes.statement: In the High-SNR regime the observations are likely to be equal to the states, or in other words, the emission matrix $R$ is close to the identity matrix $I$. We therefore write $R = I + \epsilon T$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a small constant and $T = \{t_{ij}\}$ is a matrix satisfying $t_{ii} < 0, \: t_{ij} \geq 0 , \: \forall i \neq j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{s}{t_{ij}} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: High-SNR regime: $R=I+\epsilon T$ with small $\epsilon>0$ and $T$ a zero-row-sum matrix with negative diagonal.

nodes.name: Settling of finite-system entropy coefficients (High-SNR)
nodes.statement: Let $H_N \equiv H_N(M,T,\epsilon) = H([Y]_1^N)$ be the entropy of a finite system of length $N$, and let $C_N = H_N - H_{N-1}$. Assume\footnote{It is easy to show that the functions $C_N$ are differentiable to all orders in $\epsilon$, at $\epsilon =0$. The assumption which is not proven here is that they are in fact analytic with a radius of analyticity which is uniform in N, and are uniformly bounded within some common neighborhood of $\epsilon =0$} that there is some (complex) neighborhood $B_{\rho}(0) = \{\epsilon : |\epsilon| < \rho \} \subset \mathbb{C}$ of $\epsilon=0$, in which the (one-variable) functions $\{ C_N \}, \bar{H}$ are analytic in $\epsilon$, with a Taylor expansion given by : \begin{equation} C_N(M,T,\epsilon) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} C_N^{(k)} \epsilon^k, \quad \bar{H}(M,T,\epsilon) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} C^{(k)} \epsilon^k \end{equation} \noindent (The coefficients $C_N^{(k)}$ are functions of the parameters $M$ and $T$. From now on we omit this dependence). Then: \begin{equation} N \geq \lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil \Rightarrow C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $C_N=H_N-H_{N-1}$ and $\bar H$ are analytic in $\epsilon$ near 0, the $k$-th Taylor coefficient of $C_N$ equals that of $\bar H$ once $N\ge\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil$.
assumptions: Let $H_N \equiv H_N(M,T,\epsilon) = H([Y]_1^N)$ be the entropy of a finite system of length $N$, and let $C_N = H_N - H_{N-1}$.

there is some (complex) neighborhood $B_{\rho}(0) = \{\epsilon : |\epsilon| < \rho \} \subset \mathbb{C}$ of $\epsilon=0$, in which the (one-variable) functions $\{ C_N \}, \bar{H}$ are analytic in $\epsilon$
nodes.label: high_SNR_thm

nodes.name: Han-Marcus analyticity not applicable at $\epsilon=0$
nodes.statement: The recent result (\cite{Marcus}) on analyticity of $\bar{H}$ is not applicable near $\epsilon=0$, therefore the analytic domain of $C_N$, and, more importantly $\bar{H}$, will be discussed elsewhere.

nodes.name: $C_N$ upper-bounds the entropy rate
nodes.statement: $C_N$ is actually an upperbound (\cite{Cover}) for $\bar{H}$.

nodes.name: Prior symbolic evidence for Theorem 1
nodes.statement: The behavior stated in Thm. \ref{high_SNR_thm} was discovered previously using symbolic computations, but was proven only for $k \leq 2$ , and only for the symmetric binary case (see \cite{ZKD1}).

nodes.name: Site-dependent noise process $Z$
nodes.statement: First, we distinguish between the noise parameters at different sites. This is done by considering a more general process $\{Z_N\}$, where $Z_i$'s emission matrix is $R_i = I + \epsilon_iT$. The joint distribution of $[Z]_1^N$ is thus determined by $M$,$T$ and $[\epsilon]_{1}^N$.
nodes.statement_short: Generalized process $Z$ with site-dependent emission matrices $R_i=I+\epsilon_i T$.

nodes.name: $F_N$ (entropy increment of $Z$)
nodes.statement: We define the following functions : \begin{equation} F_N(M,T,[\epsilon]_1^{N}) = H([Z]_1^N) - H([Z]_1^{N-1}) \end{equation}

nodes.name: $F_N$ at equal noise reduces to $C_N$
nodes.statement: Setting all the $\epsilon_i$'s equal, reduces us back to the $Y$ process, so in particular $F_N(M,T, (\epsilon,\ldots,\epsilon)) = C_N(\epsilon)$.

nodes.name: Blocking idea
nodes.statement: Second, we observe that if a particular $\epsilon_i$ is set to zero, the corresponding observation $Z_i$ must equal the state $X_i$. Thus, conditioning back to the past is 'blocked'.

nodes.name: Blocking lemma
nodes.statement_short: If $\epsilon_j=0$ for an interior site, $F_N$ depends only on the sites from $j$ on (the past is blocked).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement_short: Write $F_N$ as a conditional entropy and use the Markov property: $Z_j=X_j$ blocks conditioning on earlier sites.
nodes.label: F_cond_lemma

nodes.name: $F_N$ as a sum of conditional entropies
nodes.label: F_cond_eq

nodes.name: Blocking of conditional probabilities
nodes.statement: \epsilon_j = 0 \Rightarrow P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) = P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1})
nodes.label: blocking_cond

nodes.name: Write $F_N$ as conditional entropy
nodes.statement: $F$ can be written as a sum of conditional entropies : \begin{equation} F_N = -\sum_{[Z]_1^N} P([Z]_1^{N-1}) P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) \end{equation} \noindent Where the dependence on $[\epsilon]_1^N$ and $M,T$ comes through the probabilities $P(..)$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $F_N$ as a sum of conditional entropies

nodes.name: Blocking by the Markov property
nodes.statement: Since $\epsilon_j=0$, we must have $X_j = Z_j$, and therefore (since the $X_i$'s form a Markov chain), conditioning further to the past is 'blocked', that is : \begin{equation} \epsilon_j = 0 \Rightarrow P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) = P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) \end{equation} \noindent (Note that eq. (\ref{blocking_cond}) is true for $j < N$, but not for $j=N$).
nodes.statement_short: $\epsilon_j=0$ forces $Z_j=X_j$, so conditioning beyond site $j$ is blocked

nodes.name: Substitute and recognise $F_{N-j+1}$
nodes.statement: Substituting in eq. (\ref{F_cond_eq}) gives : $$ F_N = -\sum_{[Z]_1^N} P([Z]_1^{N-1}) P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) = $$ $$ -\sum_{Z_{j}^N} P([Z]_j^{N-1}) P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) $$ \begin{equation} = F_{N-j+1} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the blocked probabilities and marginalize to get $F_{N-j+1}$

nodes.name: Multi-index $\vec{k}$
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{k} = [k]_1^N$ be a vector with $k_i \in \{\mathbb{N} \cup 0\}$.

nodes.name: Weight of a multi-index
nodes.statement: Define its 'weight' as $\omega(\vec{k}) = \sum_{i=1}^N k_i$.

nodes.name: Mixed derivative $F_N^{\vec{k}}$
nodes.statement: Define also : \begin{equation} F_N^{\vec{k}} \equiv \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_N}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $F_N^{\vec{k}}$ is the mixed partial derivative of $F_N$ of orders $k_i$ in $\epsilon_i$ at $\vec\epsilon=0$.

nodes.name: Definition of $F_N^{\vec{k}}$
nodes.statement: F_N^{\vec{k}} \equiv \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_N}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0}

nodes.name: Zero-padding lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{k} = [k]_1^N$ with $k_1 \leq 1$. Denote $\vec{k}^{(r)}$ the concatenation of $\vec{k}$ with $r$ zeros : $\vec{k}^{(r)} = (\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_r,k_1,\ldots,k_N)$. Then : $$ F_N^{\vec{k}} = F_{r+N}^{\vec{k}^{(r)}} \quad, \forall r \in \mathbb{N} $$ \begin{proof} \noindent Assume first $k_1 = 0$. Using lemma \ref{F_cond_lemma}, we get : $$ F_{N+r}^{\vec{k}^{(r)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k}^{(r)})} F_{r+N}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ \begin{equation} \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_{N}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = F_N^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{r+N}) \end{equation} \noindent The case $k_1 = 1$ is reduced back to the case $k_1=0$ by taking the derivative. We denote by ${[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}$ the vector which is equal to $[Z]_1^N$ in all coordinates except on coordinate $j$, where $Z_j = r$. Using eq. (\ref{k_is_zero_eq}), we get : $$ F_{N+1}^{\vec{k}^{(1)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+1}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \left[ \left. \frac{\partial F_{N+1}}{\partial \epsilon_2} \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \right] \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N+1}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N+1}}^{(2 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) - \right. $$ $$ \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(2 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N+1} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_2^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) - \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N} = 0} = F_{N}^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_1^{N})\end{equation} \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Prepending zeros to a multi-index whose first entry is at most 1 does not change the derivative $F_N^{\vec k}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: \noindent Assume first $k_1 = 0$. Using lemma \ref{F_cond_lemma}, we get : $$ F_{N+r}^{\vec{k}^{(r)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k}^{(r)})} F_{r+N}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ \begin{equation} \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_{N}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = F_N^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{r+N}) \end{equation} \noindent The case $k_1 = 1$ is reduced back to the case $k_1=0$ by taking the derivative. We denote by ${[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}$ the vector which is equal to $[Z]_1^N$ in all coordinates except on coordinate $j$, where $Z_j = r$. Using eq. (\ref{k_is_zero_eq}), we get : $$ F_{N+1}^{\vec{k}^{(1)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+1}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \left[ \left. \frac{\partial F_{N+1}}{\partial \epsilon_2} \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \right] \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N+1}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N+1}}^{(2 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) - \right. $$ $$ \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(2 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N+1} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_2^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) - \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N} = 0} = F_{N}^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_1^{N})\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_1=0$ follows from the blocking lemma; case $k_1=1$ is reduced to it by differentiating in the first coordinate.
nodes.label: zero_tail_lemma

nodes.name: Padding for $k_1=0$
nodes.statement: \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_{N}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = F_N^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{r+N})
nodes.label: k_is_zero_eq

nodes.name: Padding for $k_1=1$
nodes.statement: \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N} = 0} = F_{N}^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_1^{N})

nodes.name: Case $k_1=0$
nodes.statement: Assume first $k_1 = 0$. Using lemma \ref{F_cond_lemma}, we get : $$ F_{N+r}^{\vec{k}^{(r)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k}^{(r)})} F_{r+N}([\epsilon]_1^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ \begin{equation} \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_{N}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{N+r})}{\partial \epsilon_{r+2}^{k_2},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_{r+N}^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = F_N^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_{r+1}^{r+N}) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_1=0$: apply the blocking lemma to drop the zero sites

nodes.name: Case $k_1=1$: reduction
nodes.statement: The case $k_1 = 1$ is reduced back to the case $k_1=0$ by taking the derivative. We denote by ${[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}$ the vector which is equal to $[Z]_1^N$ in all coordinates except on coordinate $j$, where $Z_j = r$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_1=1$: reduce to $k_1=0$ by taking the derivative; introduce $[Z]^{(j\to r)}$

nodes.name: Compute the derivative and shift
nodes.statement: Using eq. (\ref{k_is_zero_eq}), we get : $$ F_{N+1}^{\vec{k}^{(1)}}([\epsilon]_1^{N+1}) = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \left[ \left. \frac{\partial F_{N+1}}{\partial \epsilon_2} \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \right] \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_3^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N+1}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N+1}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N+1}}^{(2 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) - \right. $$ $$ \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N+1} | [Z]_1^{N}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(2 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_2 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N+1} = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_2^{k_2} \dots \partial \epsilon_{N}^{k_N}} \Biggl\{ - \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_1^{N}} $$ $$ \left[ P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \log P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) - \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. \left. P(Z_{N} | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0} \Biggr\} \right|_{[\epsilon]_1^{N} = 0} = F_{N}^{\vec{k}}([\epsilon]_1^{N})\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate in $\epsilon_2$, apply the $k_1=0$ case and shift indices

nodes.name: $C_N^{(k)}$ as sum of mixed derivatives
nodes.statement: $C_N^{(k)}$ is obtained by summing $F_N^{\vec{k}}$ on all $\vec{k}$'s with weight $k$ : \begin{equation} C_N^{(k)} = \sum_{\vec{k},\omega(\vec{k})=k} F_N^{\vec{k}} \end{equation}

nodes.name: $C_N^{(k)} = \sum F_N^{\vec{k}}$
nodes.statement: C_N^{(k)} = \sum_{\vec{k},\omega(\vec{k})=k} F_N^{\vec{k}}

nodes.name: No-hole lemma
nodes.statement_short: A mixed derivative vanishes if some earlier site has order $\ge1$ and a later non-final site has order $\le1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_j=0$: blocking removes dependence on $\epsilon_i$. Case $k_j=1$: differentiate $P(Z)$ in $\epsilon_j$ and show the derivative of $F_N$ is blocked from earlier sites.
nodes.label: No_hole_strong_lemma

nodes.name: Vanishing for $k_j=0$
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots, \partial \epsilon_i^{k_i-1},\ldots, \partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \left[\left. \frac{\partial F_{N-j+1}([\epsilon]_j^N)}{\partial \epsilon_i} \right] \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = 0

nodes.name: Probability of $Z$ via $X$
nodes.statement: \sum_{[X]_1^N} P([X]_1^N) \prod_{i=1}^N (\delta_{X_i Z_i} + \epsilon_i t_{X_i Z_i})

nodes.name: Derivative of $P(Z)$ in $\epsilon_j$
nodes.statement: \left. \left\{ \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) \right\} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0}

nodes.name: Derivative of conditional probability
nodes.statement: \left. \left. P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1} ) P({[Z]_1^{N-1}}^{(j \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0}

nodes.name: Derivative of $P\log P$
nodes.statement: \left. \left. P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) - P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N-1}}^{(j \to r)})\right\} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0}

nodes.name: Derivative of $F_N$ in $\epsilon_j$
nodes.statement: \left. \left. P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) P({[Z]_j^{N-1}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \Biggr\} \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0}
nodes.label: F_N_deriv_eq

nodes.name: Case $k_j=0$
nodes.statement: Assume first $k_j = 0$. Using lemma \ref{F_cond_lemma} we get $$ F_N^{\vec{k}} \equiv \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_N(\vec{\epsilon})}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = \left. \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})} F_{N-j+1}([\epsilon]_j^N)}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots,\partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = $$ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial^{\omega(\vec{k})-1}}{\partial \epsilon_1^{k_1},\ldots, \partial \epsilon_i^{k_i-1},\ldots, \partial \epsilon_N^{k_N}} \left[\left. \frac{\partial F_{N-j+1}([\epsilon]_j^N)}{\partial \epsilon_i} \right] \right|_{\vec{\epsilon} = 0} = 0 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_j=0$: by the blocking lemma $F_N$ does not depend on $\epsilon_i$, so the derivative vanishes

nodes.name: Case $k_j=1$
nodes.statement_short: Case $k_j=1$: the $\epsilon_j$-derivative of $F_N$ is blocked from earlier sites

nodes.name: Write $P(Z)$ through $X$
nodes.statement: The case $k_j = 1$ is more difficult, but follows the same principles. Write the probability of $Z$ : $$ P([Z]_1^N) = \sum_{[X]_1^N} P([X]_1^N) P([Z]_1^N | [X]_1^N) = $$ \begin{equation} \sum_{[X]_1^N} P([X]_1^N) \prod_{i=1}^N (\delta_{X_i Z_i} + \epsilon_i t_{X_i Z_i})\end{equation} \noindent where $\delta_{ij}$ is Kronecker delta.
nodes.statement_short: Write $P([Z]_1^N)$ as a sum over hidden paths

nodes.name: Differentiate $P(Z)$
nodes.statement: Write now the derivative with respect to $\epsilon_j$: $$ \left. \frac{\partial P([Z]_1^N)}{\partial \epsilon_j} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ $$ \left. \sum_{[X]_1^N} \left[ P([X]_1^N) t_{X_j Z_j} \prod_{i \neq j} (\delta_{X_i Z_i} + \epsilon_i t_{X_i Z_i}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left\{ \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) \right\} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $P(Z)$ with respect to $\epsilon_j$ at $\epsilon_j=0$

nodes.name: Bayes' rule
nodes.statement: Using Bayes' rule $P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) = \frac{P([Z]_1^N)}{P([Z]_1^{N-1})}$, we get : $$ \left. \frac{\partial P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1})}{\partial \epsilon_j} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ $$ \frac{1}{P([Z]_1^{N-1})} \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \left[ P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) - \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1} ) P({[Z]_1^{N-1}}^{(j \to r)}) \right] \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use Bayes' rule to differentiate the conditional probability

nodes.name: Derivative of $P\log P$
nodes.statement: This gives : $$ \left. \frac{\partial [P([Z]_1^N) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1})]}{\partial \epsilon_j} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ $$ \sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \left\{ P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) + \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) - P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N-1}}^{(j \to r)})\right\} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Derivative of $P\log P(Z_N|\cdot)$

nodes.name: Blocked derivative of $F_N$
nodes.statement: And therefore : $$ \left. \frac{\partial F_N}{\partial \epsilon_j} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ $$ -\sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \Biggl\{ \sum_{[Z]_1^N} \left[ P({[Z]_1^N}^{(j \to r)}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) - \right. $$ $$ \left. \left. P(Z_N | [Z]_1^{N-1}) P({[Z]_1^{N-1}}^{(j \to r)}) \right] \Biggr\} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0} = $$ $$ \Biggl\{ -\sum_{r=1}^{s} t_{X_i r} \sum_{[Z]_j^N} \left[ P({[Z]_j^N}^{(1 \to r)}) \log P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) - \right. $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left. P(Z_N | [Z]_j^{N-1}) P({[Z]_j^{N-1}}^{(1 \to r)}) \right] \Biggr\} \right|_{\epsilon_1 = 0} \end{equation} \noindent Where the latter equality comes from using eq. (\ref{blocking_cond}), which 'blocks' the dependence backwards.
nodes.statement_short: Combine and use the blocking equation to restrict to sites $j..N$

nodes.name: Conclude vanishing
nodes.statement: Eq. \ref{F_N_deriv_eq} shows that $\left. \frac{\partial F_N}{\partial \epsilon_j} \right|_{\epsilon_j = 0}$ does not depend on $\epsilon_i$ for $i < j$, therefore $\frac{\partial^{k_i+1} F_N}{\partial \epsilon_i^{k_i} \partial \epsilon_j} = 0$ and $F_N^{\vec{k}} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The derivative does not depend on $\epsilon_i$, $i<j$, hence $F_N^{\vec k}=0$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 bounds the support length of nonzero $F_N^{\vec k}$, Lemma 2 shows they equal those of $N=\lceil(k+3)/2\rceil$; summing and analyticity give the limit.
nodes.label: strong_thm

nodes.name: Reduction to length $\lceil (k+3)/2 \rceil$
nodes.statement: F_N^{\vec{k}} = F_{\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil}^{(k_{N-\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil+1},\ldots,{k_N})}

nodes.name: Define length of $\vec k$
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{k} = [k]_1^N$ with $\omega(\vec{k}) = k$. Define its 'length' (from right, considering only entries larger than one) as $l(\vec{k}) = N+1-\min_{k_i > 1} \{i \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the length $l(\vec k)$ of a multi-index of weight $k$

nodes.name: Bound the length
nodes.statement: It easily follows from lemma \ref{No_hole_strong_lemma} that if $F_N^{\vec{k}} \neq 0$, we must have $l(\vec{k}) \leq \lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3, a nonzero $F_N^{\vec k}$ has length at most $\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil-1$

nodes.name: Pad to a short system
nodes.statement: Therefore, according to lemma \ref{zero_tail_lemma} we have : \begin{equation} F_N^{\vec{k}} = F_{\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil}^{(k_{N-\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil+1},\ldots,{k_N})} \end{equation} \noindent for all $\vec{k}$'s in the sum.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2 each nonzero term equals one of the system of length $\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil$

nodes.name: Sum over weight $k$
nodes.statement: Summing on all $F_N^{\vec{k}}$ with the same 'weight', we get $C_N^{(k)} = C_{\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil}^{(k)}, \quad \forall N > \lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$.
nodes.statement_short: Summing gives $C_N^{(k)}=C_{\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil}^{(k)}$ for larger $N$

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: From the analyticity of $C_N$ and $\bar{H}$ around $\epsilon=0$, one can show by induction that $\lim_{N \to \infty} C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)}$, therefore we must have $C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)}, \quad \forall N \geq \lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil $.

nodes.name: Entropy rate
nodes.statement: \bar{H}(Y) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{H([Y]_1^N)}{N}

nodes.name: Taylor expansions of $C_N$ and $\bar H$ in $\epsilon$

nodes.name: Almost-Memoryless (A-M) regime
nodes.statement: In the A-M regime, the Markov transition matrix is close to uniform. Thus, throughout this section, we assume that $M$ is given by $M = U + \delta T$, such that $U$ is a constant (uniform) matrix, $u_{ij} = s^{-1}$, $\delta > 0$ is a small constant and $T$ satisfies $\sum_{j=1}^{s}{t_{ij}} = 0$.

nodes.name: Analyticity and settling of coefficients (Almost-Memoryless)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof of analyticity relies on the recent result, namely Thm. 1.1 in \cite{Marcus}. In order to use this result, we need to present the {\it HMP} $Y$ in the following way : We introduce the new alphabet $\Gamma \subset \Sigma \times \Sigma $ defined by : $$ \Gamma = \Big\{ w = (w_x,w_y) : w_x,w_y \in \Sigma, r_{w_x w_y} > 0 \Big\} $$ We also introduce the function $\Phi : \Gamma \to \Sigma$, defined by $\Phi(w) \equiv \Phi(w_x,w_y) = w_y$. Let $w,v \in \Gamma$ with $w = (w_x, w_y), v = (v_x,v_y)$. One can look at the new Markov process $W = (X,Y)$, defined on $\Gamma$ by the transition matrix $\Delta_{|\Gamma| \times |\Gamma|}$, which is given by $\Delta_{wv} \equiv P(W_{N+1} = v | W_N = w) = m_{w_x v_x} r_{v_x v_y}$. Then the process $Y$ can be defined as $Y_N = \Phi(W_N)$. Using the above representation, clearly $\Delta$ is analytically parameterized by $\delta$. Moreover, there is some (real) neighborhood $B_{\rho'}(0) \subset \mathbb{R}$ in which all of $\Delta$'s entries are positive. Therefore, Thm. 1.1 from \cite{Marcus} applies here, and according to its proof, $\{C_N\}$ and $\bar{H}$ are analytic (as functions of $\delta$) in some complex neighborhood $B_{\rho}(0) \subset \mathbb{C}$ of zero. \item The proof of part 2 is very similar to that of Thm. \ref{high_SNR_thm}. Distinguishing between the sites by setting $M_i = U + \delta_i T$ in site $i$, we notice that if one sets $\delta_i = 0$ for some $i$, then $M_i$ becomes uniform, and thus knowing $Z_i$ 'blocks' the dependence of $Z_N$ on previous $Z_j$'s ($\forall j < i$). The rest of the proof continues in an analogous way to the proof of Thm. \ref{high_SNR_thm} (including the three lemmas therein), and its details are thus omitted here. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: Our method for computing $C^{(k)}$ is straightforward. We compute $C_N^{(k)}$ for $N = \lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$ by simply enumerating all sequences $[Y]_1^N$, computing the $k$-th coefficient in $P([Y]_1^N) \log P([Y]_1^N)$ for each one, and summing their contribution.

nodes.statement: Let $M = U + \delta T$. (\ref{general_alphabet_ hmm_entropy})) in $\delta$. $M$ is simply replaced by $U + \delta T$. Dealing with $\pi$ is more problematic. Note that the stationary distribution of $U$ is $s^{-1} \xi$. We write $\pi = s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi + O(\delta^2)$, and solve : \begin{equation} (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) (U + \delta T) = (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) + O(\delta^2) \end{equation} \noindent It follows that $\psi$ should satisfy $\psi (I - U) = \xi T$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. We cannot invert $I-U$ since it is of rank $s-1$. The extra equation needed for determining $\psi$ uniquely comes from the requirement $\sum_{i=1}^s \psi_i = 0$. Substituting $M =U + \delta T$ and $\pi = s^{-1} \xi + \psi \delta + O(\delta^2)$ in eq. (\ref{general_alphabet_ hmm_entropy}), one gets : $$ C_2 = \Big\{log(s^{-1} \xi R) s^{-1} R^t U R - $$ $$ \xi^t [(s^{-1} R^t U R) .* log (s^{-1} R^t U R)] \Big\} \xi + $$ $$ \bigg\{\log (s^{-1} \xi R) R^t [s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U] R - $$ $$ \xi^t \Big[ \Big(R^t (s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U) R \Big) .* $$ \begin{equation} \Big( s U + \log(s^{-1} R^t U R)\Big) \Big] \bigg \} \xi \delta + O(\delta^2) \end{equation} \noindent After further simplification, most terms in eq. \ref{almost_memoryless_inter_eq} cancel out, and we are left with the result (\ref{prop_weak_memory}). \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: First-order expansion of $\bar H$ in $\delta$ for $M=U+\delta T$ and a general alphabet; generically linear in $\delta$.

We cannot invert $I-U$ since it is of rank $s-1$. The extra equation needed for determining $\psi$ uniquely comes from the requirement $\sum_{i=1}^s \psi_i = 0$. Substituting $M =U + \delta T$ and $\pi = s^{-1} \xi + \psi \delta + O(\delta^2)$ in eq. (\ref{general_alphabet_ hmm_entropy}), one gets : $$ C_2 = \Big\{log(s^{-1} \xi R) s^{-1} R^t U R - $$ $$ \xi^t [(s^{-1} R^t U R) .* log (s^{-1} R^t U R)] \Big\} \xi + $$ $$ \bigg\{\log (s^{-1} \xi R) R^t [s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U] R - $$ $$ \xi^t \Big[ \Big(R^t (s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U) R \Big) .* $$ \begin{equation} \Big( s U + \log(s^{-1} R^t U R)\Big) \Big] \bigg \} \xi \delta + O(\delta^2) \end{equation} \noindent After further simplification, most terms in eq. \ref{almost_memoryless_inter_eq} cancel out, and we are left with the result (\ref{prop_weak_memory}).
nodes.statement_short: Expand $C_2$ in $\delta$, with $\pi=s^{-1}\xi+\delta\psi$ found from a perturbed stationarity equation; terms cancel to the result.
nodes.label: almost_memoryless_first_order

nodes.name: Perturbed stationarity equation
nodes.statement: (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) (U + \delta T) = (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) + O(\delta^2)

nodes.name: First-order expansion of $C_2$ in $\delta$
nodes.statement: \Big( s U + \log(s^{-1} R^t U R)\Big) \Big] \bigg \} \xi \delta + O(\delta^2)
nodes.label: almost_memoryless_inter_eq

nodes.name: Reduce to $C_2$
nodes.statement: Since $\bar{H} = C_2 + O(\delta^2)$, we expand $C_2$ (as given in eq. (\ref{general_alphabet_ hmm_entropy})) in $\delta$. $M$ is simply replaced by $U + \delta T$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\bar H=C_2+O(\delta^2)$, expand $C_2$ with $M=U+\delta T$

nodes.name: Perturb $\pi$
nodes.statement: Dealing with $\pi$ is more problematic. Note that the stationary distribution of $U$ is $s^{-1} \xi$. We write $\pi = s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi + O(\delta^2)$, and solve : \begin{equation} (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) (U + \delta T) = (s^{-1} \xi + \delta \psi) + O(\delta^2) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\pi=s^{-1}\xi+\delta\psi$ and impose stationarity

nodes.name: Solve for $\psi$
nodes.statement: It follows that $\psi$ should satisfy $\psi (I - U) = \xi T$, where $I$ is the identity matrix. We cannot invert $I-U$ since it is of rank $s-1$. The extra equation needed for determining $\psi$ uniquely comes from the requirement $\sum_{i=1}^s \psi_i = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Determine $\psi$ from $\psi(I-U)=\xi T$ and $\sum\psi_i=0$

nodes.name: Substitute into $C_2$
nodes.statement: Substituting $M =U + \delta T$ and $\pi = s^{-1} \xi + \psi \delta + O(\delta^2)$ in eq. (\ref{general_alphabet_ hmm_entropy}), one gets : $$ C_2 = \Big\{log(s^{-1} \xi R) s^{-1} R^t U R - $$ $$ \xi^t [(s^{-1} R^t U R) .* log (s^{-1} R^t U R)] \Big\} \xi + $$ $$ \bigg\{\log (s^{-1} \xi R) R^t [s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U] R - $$ $$ \xi^t \Big[ \Big(R^t (s^{-1} diag(\xi) T + diag(\psi) U) R \Big) .* $$ \begin{equation} \Big( s U + \log(s^{-1} R^t U R)\Big) \Big] \bigg \} \xi \delta + O(\delta^2) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into the matrix form of $C_2$

nodes.name: Simplify
nodes.statement: After further simplification, most terms in eq. \ref{almost_memoryless_inter_eq} cancel out, and we are left with the result (\ref{prop_weak_memory}).
nodes.statement_short: Cancellations give the proposition

nodes.name: Consistency with Ordentlich-Weissman and linear behaviour
nodes.statement: In \cite{Weissman:01} it was shown that the first order term vanishes for the symmetric binary case, which is consistent with eq. \ref{prop_weak_memory}. Our result holds for general alphabets and process parameters. Looking at the symmetric binary case might be misleading here, since by doing so one fails to see the linear behavior in $\delta$ for the general case.

nodes.name: Almost-memoryless series for the symmetric binary HMP up to $O(\delta^{14})$
nodes.statement: We have computed higher orders for the symmetric binary case by expanding $C_N$ for $N=8$, which gives us $C^{(k)}$ for $k \leq 13$. In this case the expansion is in the parameter $\delta = \frac{1}{2}-p$, and gives (for better readability the dependency on $\epsilon$ is represented here via $\mu = 1-2\epsilon$) : $$ \bar{H} = \log(2) - \mu^4 \bigg[2 \delta^2 + \frac{4}{3} (7 \mu^4-12 \mu^2+6) \delta^4+ $$ $$ \frac{32}{15}(46 \mu^8-120 \mu^6+120 \mu^4-60 \mu^2+15) \delta^6 + $$ $$ \frac{32}{21}(1137 \mu^{12}-4088\mu^{10}+5964 \mu^8-4536 \mu^6+1946 \mu^4- $$ $$ 504 \mu^2+84) \delta^8 + \frac{512}{45} (3346 \mu^{16}-15120 \mu^{14}+28800 \mu^{12}- $$ $$ 30120 \mu^{10}+18990 \mu^8 - 7560 \mu^6+1980 \mu^4-360 \mu^2+45) \delta^{10} + $$ $$ \frac{1024}{165} (159230 \mu^{20}-874632 \mu^{18}+ 2091100 \mu^{16}-2857360 \mu^{14}+ $$ $$ 2465100 \mu^{12}-1400960 \mu^{10}+532312 \mu^8-135960 \mu^6+ $$ \begin{equation} 24145 \mu^4- 3300 \mu^2+330) \delta^{12} \bigg] + O(\delta^{14}) ; \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $C_8$ gives $\bar H$ in $\delta=1/2-p$ to order 13 for the symmetric binary HMP, with $\mu=1-2\epsilon$.
assumptions: the expansion is in the parameter $\delta = \frac{1}{2}-p$

nodes.name: Ordentlich-Weissman second-order A-M asymptotics
nodes.statement: The above expansion generalizes a result from \cite{Weissman:01}, who proved $\bar{H} = \log(2) - 2 \mu^4 \delta^2 + o(\delta^2)$.

nodes.name: Odd powers vanish in the A-M series
nodes.statement: Note that for the first few coefficients, all odd powers of $\delta$ vanish, and the coefficients are all polynomials of $\mu^2$, which makes this series simpler than the one obtained in the High-SNR regime (\cite{ZKD1}).

nodes.name: Radius of convergence and analyticity domain
nodes.statement: The usefulness of a series expansion such as the ones derived in eq. (\ref{series_almost_memoryless}) and in \cite{ZKD1} for practical purposes, highly depends on the radius of convergence. Determining the radius is a difficult problem, as it relates to the domain of analyticity of $\bar{H}$. In Thm. \ref{almost_memoryless_thm} we proved that the radius for the A-M expansion is positive.

nodes.name: A-M expansion has much larger estimated radius
nodes.statement: For the High-SNR case, we gave a numerical estimation of the radius of convergence $\rho(p)$ as a function of $p$ (\cite{ZKD2}), based on the first few known terms. When one applies the same procedure to the coefficients of the A-M expansion, the numerical values of the estimated radius are much higher.
conclusions: the numerical values of the estimated radius are much higher

nodes.name: Upper and lower bounds on the HMP entropy rate
nodes.statement: In this figure, the (finite) series expansions with up to twelve'th order is compared to two known bounds on $\bar{H}$ from \cite{Cover}. The upper bound is simply $C_N = H(Y_N | [Y]_1^{N-1})$ and the lower bound is $c_N \equiv H(Y_N | X_1, [Y]_1^{N-1})$, for $N=2$.
conclusions: The upper bound is simply $C_N = H(Y_N | [Y]_1^{N-1})$ and the lower bound is $c_N \equiv H(Y_N | X_1, [Y]_1^{N-1})$

nodes.name: Finite-order expansions versus bounds
nodes.statement: As can be seen from the figure, for the High-SNR case at $p=0.2$, the finite-order expansions are not within the bounds for large values of $\epsilon$. For the A-M case, for $\epsilon=0.2$, the finite-order expansions remain within the bounds for any $0<p<\frac{1}{2}$.
conclusions: the finite-order expansions are not within the bounds for large values of $\epsilon$
the finite-order expansions remain within the bounds for any $0<p<\frac{1}{2}$

nodes.name: Real analyticity of the binary HMP entropy rate (Han-Marcus)
nodes.statement: In our context, the result of \cite{Marcus} proves that $\bar{H}(p,\epsilon)$ is real analytic in the domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2, \quad \Omega = \{(p,\epsilon): 0<p,\epsilon<1 \}$ (it is not known whether $\Omega$ is maximal with that respect).
conclusions: $\bar{H}(p,\epsilon)$ is real analytic in the domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2, \quad \Omega = \{(p,\epsilon): 0<p,\epsilon<1 \}$

nodes.name: A-M expansion is interior, High-SNR on the boundary
nodes.statement: For any $0<\epsilon<1$, the A-M expansion is near the point $(\epsilon, \frac{1}{2})$ which is an interior point of $\Omega$. The High-SNR expansion is near some point $(p,0)$, which lies on the boundary of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Weaker settling for conditional-probability functionals
nodes.statement: For other functions involving only conditional probabilities (e.g. relative entropy between two {\it HMPs}) a weaker result holds: the coefficients 'settle' for $N \geq k$.
assumptions: For other functions involving only conditional probabilities (e.g. relative entropy between two {\it HMPs})

nodes.name: No finite-chain approximation in the rare-transitions regime
nodes.statement: We note that this is still a highly non-trivial result, as it is known that for other regimes (e.g. 'rare-transitions' \cite{Weissman:03}), a finite chain of any length does not give the correct asymptotic behavior even to the first order.
conclusions: a finite chain of any length does not give the correct asymptotic behavior even to the first order
